title: Ep 289: Navigating 'Unruliness': Hence Cofounder Sean West on How Politics, AI and Law are Rewriting Business Rules
author: Sean West

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: West shifts the focus from AI-enabled legal workflows, specialist model layers and lawyer verification to buyer-side technology for selecting, valuing and managing professional advice. Hence’s evolution into outside-counsel, matter and litigation management offers a materially different commercial framing rather than evidence for or against the cluster’s core AI proposition.
qs: In our initial product suite was really focused on how people buy advice.
We were heads down like legal tech focused company on outside council management which evolved into broader matter management, litigation management for a handful of years.

st.t: Adoption leadership: Trust must follow customer outcomes
st.an: The source contains only closing remarks and provides no substantive claims, evidence, predictions or recommendations with which to assess its position on cautious AI adoption, provider collaboration, earned trust, customer outcomes or distributed expertise.

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: The supplied source contains only closing remarks, feedback and production credits, with no substantive claims about pragmatic AI adoption, experimentation, transformation evidence, implementation, or future workflows. There is therefore insufficient evidence to assess its position relative to the cluster proposition.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: West supports the cluster’s core view that AI will automate parts of legal production while increasing the importance of lawyers’ strategic judgment and client-focused advice. His claims are predictive and qualitative, consistent with the synthesis’s caution that market-wide transformation remains unproven.
qs: The necessity for lawyers to be strategic advisors is going to increase because that's going to be their differentiation against most of the AI tools that are doing parts of the legal supply chain, value chain.
What a lot of lawyers end up doing is kind of retreating into their traditional client work and not thinking as strategically as necessary about what's going on in the world to advise their clients.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: West directly supports the proposition that AI will automate parts of legal production while increasing, rather than eliminating, the value of lawyers. He predicts that lawyers will differentiate themselves through strategic advice and broader situational awareness, though he does not substantively address the cluster’s pricing, buyer-side reallocation or provider-model claims.
qs: The necessity for lawyers to be strategic advisors is going to increase because that's going to be their differentiation against most of the AI tools that are doing parts of the legal supply chain, value chain.
What a lot of lawyers end up doing is kind of retreating into their traditional client work and not thinking as strategically as necessary about what's going on in the world to advise their clients.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: West broadly supports selective, task-level deployment: he presents AI as handling bounded assistance such as demand-letter drafting and personalised information filtering while arguing that lawyers become more, not less, important. His evidence is largely anecdotal and does not substantively address verification, capability limits or operating-model redesign.
qs: Well, I think the role of the lawyer is increasingly important in this type of world.
They literally just created a demand letter for me in the right language.

kp.k: Intersecting disruptions require integrated legal and business strategy
kp.d: West's central framework is that the retreat of globalization's rules coincides with changes in law and AI, producing risks that cannot be understood through separate disciplinary forecasts. He presents this as the thesis of his book, not a measured finding, and sees opportunities alongside risks.
qs: The rules and norms that were developed during globalization are falling away.

So the kind of core thesis of the book is that politics, AI, and law are all changing at once, yet most of us are organized only to fight these as individual factors, and the future will be characterized by the risks that emerge from the clash of these factors.

kp.k: Geo-legal risks strengthen the strategic role of in-house lawyers
kp.d: West argues that political shocks generate sanctions, asset disposal, employment and intellectual-property questions, making legal involvement necessary before crises rather than afterward. He cites the aftermath of Russia's invasion of Ukraine and uses a hypothetical Chinese declaration concerning Taiwanese law to illustrate anticipatory planning. He reports an increasing tendency for government affairs, risk, ethics and formerly ESG functions to report into legal departments, endorsing that organizational direction.
qs: what I call geo-legal risk, that's at the intersection of politics and law.
there's a lot of geo-legal strategic planning you could do today.
And we've seen law departments increasingly take on their reporting lines for government affairs, for risk, for what was ESG, for ethics, right?

kp.k: Executive volatility increases reliance on legal judgment and courts
kp.d: West characterizes the contemporary US environment as unusually self-inflicted political volatility, with concentrated executive power reducing businesses' ability to anticipate policy. In his account, lawyers help companies navigate transactional political engagement without exchanging one risk for another, while courts become a principal avenue for challenging executive action. His scenarios about future deportations and tax changes are hypothetical, not reported outcomes.
qs: I think what we're experiencing now is the most self-inflicted volatility I've ever seen politically
When you're in a world like that, you need lawyers who can help you understand what you can do and what you can't do, right?
We're living in a world where anything you can imagine can happen because it's one person's idea effectuated through executive order and then negotiated in the courts to restrain it.

kp.k: AI could broaden access to expensive geopolitical advice
kp.d: West argues that even small businesses have global exposure through products, suppliers or clients, while traditional bespoke advice is prohibitively expensive for much of this market. His commercial thesis is that technology can supply much of the information these businesses need at close to zero marginal cost per user; the wealthiest clients will still pay for expert human access. This concerns business advisory access, distinct from access to justice.
qs: All of them, this is my thesis, all of them would pay a dollar to understand how the world is impacting their business so that they can get an advantage. What they're unwilling to do is spend a million dollars on that advice.
Look, the biggest companies have the most resources, and the richest people always pay to talk to the smartest humans.
But technology can actually serve a lot of the market by helping people understand most of what they need to know. And technology does that at close to zero marginal cost per user.

kp.k: Personalized AI monitoring supports proactive client advice
kp.d: Describing Hence Global as its cofounder, West says the platform ingests and classifies news, combines public organizational information with users' stated interests, and delivers personalized daily briefings with further research capabilities. He reports a handful of early-adopter law firms and emphasizes differentiation by practice area and client portfolio. These are product and adoption claims, without independent performance evidence in the transcript.
qs: We've got a handful of great early adopter law firms that have been working with us on it, as well as other use cases.

So what we've done is built a system that ingests the world's news, classifies it, understands you based on public source information about your organization and what you tell it about yourself and what you're interested in, and then delivers you a personal daily briefing of the things you need to know that matter to you, along with the ability to go way deeper within the tool.

kp.k: Monitoring augments lawyers rather than replacing their substantive advice
kp.d: West positions Hence Global as a way to identify otherwise missed political developments with legal implications, leaving lawyers to interpret the implications and advise clients. He argues that technology's broader recall of client operations can help lawyers initiate timely conversations and become trusted advisers, rather than merely respond to instructions.
qs: But the reality is the system's not trying to replace your advice.

The system's trying to tell you on story number seven today, on the weak signal that you would miss, there's an employment law ramification that you didn't understand, and that you would be able to understand it and advise your clients.
So you as a lawyer can use tools to actually keep track of how politics is impacting your clients and see that as a way to be the first phone call to them, the way to be the trusted advisor to them.

kp.k: AI extends monitoring into analysis and legal marketing
kp.d: West says the platform combines current news with historical context and is being used to draft client alerts and branded newsletters. He reports that an experimental daily AI-generated Hence newsletter grew from zero to a thousand followers in less than a week; this is a personal adoption anecdote, not evidence of analytical accuracy. Market-entry studies, travel-security briefings and scenario development are described as future product directions.
qs: But beyond that, it serves as an analytical tool. It also serves as a marketing tool.

So law firms are using it to draft client alerts, because if the system can develop a point of view about how a news story matters for a client, that saves the law firm the need to develop that client alert.
We went from zero to a thousand followers in less than a week, right?

kp.k: Legal automation increases pressure to differentiate through strategic advice
kp.d: West predicts that automation of portions of legal work will increase lawyers' need to act as strategic advisers. He identifies political, legal and technological situational awareness as a basis for that differentiation and for selecting which disputes or regulatory interventions matter to clients. The transcript supplies no quantified forecast of employment, staffing or revenue effects.
qs: The necessity for lawyers to be strategic advisors is going to increase because that's going to be their differentiation against most of the AI tools that are doing parts of the legal supply chain, value chain.
It's not about picking every battle. It's about understanding what really matters to your business.

kp.k: AI-generated demands can improve individuals' negotiating power
kp.d: West recounts using an AI-powered bot from Zaf Legal, which he describes as regulated in Utah, after an insurer disputed his diagnosed concussion. He says sending its demand letter led the insurer to increase its initial offer tenfold within minutes. He also reports generating a complaint separately. He presents this personal pre-litigation experience as an access-to-justice benefit and asserts that no unauthorized practice occurred; the transcript does not establish that as a general legal conclusion.
qs: I found Zaf Legal, regulated out of Utah, which has an AI-powered bot, and I took the demand letter and I sent it to the insurance company.
Within minutes, they 10x the initial offer that they had made to me.
Now, that's pre-litigation. There's no unauthorized practice of law. They literally just created a demand letter for me in the right language.

kp.k: Courtroom automation illustrates alternative routes to legal access
kp.d: West reports that Chinese courtroom legal robots let users enter a case, receive a likelihood-of-success estimate and initiate a claim. He uses a 70% likelihood as an illustrative interface output, not a measured accuracy rate, and says the system encourages settlement. His argument is that conceptions of legal service delivery, rather than technical feasibility alone, constrain deployment.
qs: I've written about in China, they have legal robots in the courtrooms that you can punch in your case if you want to sue someone. It'll tell you you're 70% likely to win, would you like to file the claim now?
Now, the system's kind of wired to get you to settle because they want like a harmonious society, but it's up to you whether you want to file the claim, it'll file it for you.
So the tech hasn't been the barrier to doing this. I think it's our conception of it.

kp.k: Cheap automated filings may weaponize legal and regulatory processes
kp.d: West predicts that near-costless lawsuit generation could enable millions of hostile claims and warns about fraudulent or frivolous filings. As a related reported example, he says crypto-lawyer activists used a bot to generate over 100,000 comments on a Biden-era Treasury crypto-brokering proposal, delaying the rule until a different political environment arrived. His causal account is not independently substantiated in the transcript. Host Bob Ambrogi separately introduces the framing of a 'distributed denial of justice attack.'
qs: when it costs nothing to file lawsuits against people, you're going to start to see millions of lawsuits pointed at your enemies, pointed at you if you're someone's enemy.
But on the negative side, there's a huge amount of risk from flooding people with fraudulent claims or with frivolous claims.
They generated over 100,000 comments and Treasury by law has to consider all of them.
They ground a rule the federal government wanted to halt until a new political environment came about.

kp.k: Synthetic media threatens evidentiary trust through the liar's dividend
kp.d: West identifies erosion of shared truth as a central AI risk: exposure to fabricated material can make authentic evidence easier to deny. He attributes the term 'liar's dividend' to lawyers and recounts a defense involving a video of Elon Musk discussing Tesla autodrive safety. He treats the episode as illustrating potential evidentiary and social consequences, not as establishing a judicial rule on authentication or burdens of proof.
qs: The real risk is that we erode the concept of truth itself.
But the problem is that when you're exposed to so much fake stuff, you start to believe true things are fake.
And his lawyer's defense was, you can't prove that video is not a deep fake.
the idea that anyone could just assert that the burden is on you to prove a video is not a deep fake is a pretty chilling thought.

kp.k: AI can amplify state surveillance and political control
kp.d: Beyond deepfakes and hallucinations, West warns that AI makes accumulated government data easier to use for surveillance and classification of citizens. He invokes China's social credit system and says he sees some movement in this direction in the US. These are his cross-domain political-risk assertions, without supporting study details in the interview.
qs: AI can be an accelerant on good things and it can be an accelerant on bad things.
When the government's collected lots of data on its citizens, the ability to use AI to surveil and sort people into good and bad lists is very, very easy.

kp.k: Sub-enterprise businesses face strategic legal capability gaps
kp.d: West judges large companies relatively prepared because they have developed intelligence and legal teams, while businesses around $100 million or $1 billion in revenue can remain exposed without recognizing it. He illustrates the gap with a $500 million-revenue business employing five lawyers primarily on operational work. He sees demand for strategic general counsel with political expertise and a career opportunity for mid-career lawyers who acquire that expertise; these are practitioner judgments rather than survey findings.
qs: I think big companies are in a pretty good position because the world's been on Unruly for quite some time.
These companies that are the ones who are most exposed without understanding it, they're the ones who have never invested in having a strategic in-house legal department.

I think a lot of them are waking up to the fact that they need strategic general counsel, but there's not enough strategic general counsel who've cut their teeth in the political world floating around.

kp.k: Lawyers should audit knowledge sources and learn across disciplines
kp.d: West recommends examining the 'knowledge supply chain': sources of news and analysis, biases, adviser selection, confidentiality arrangements and possible exclusivity in advance of crises. He urges lawyers to seek genuine external domain expertise through conferences and executive education rather than relying exclusively on legal intermediaries. He presents broader geopolitical learning as part of professional upskilling for a less siloed environment.
qs: Do you actually understand how your team is getting its news and its insights?
Because if bias is creeping into the analysis that you're then relying on, you will get it wrong.
And honestly, Bob, the biggest advice for lawyers is get out of your domain to get that advice.
I think that we live in a world that is no longer siloed and if the legal community thinks of themselves as being in a silo, they will get smacked in ways that are really painful.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Sean West presents AI as both an enabler of cheaper, more proactive advice and a source of litigation abuse and evidentiary distrust. He predicts that automation will increase lawyers' need to differentiate themselves as strategic advisors.
pts.d:
1. Broader access to advice: West argues that technology can supply much of the geopolitical understanding businesses need at close to zero marginal cost per user, serving buyers priced out of traditional expert advice, while wealthy buyers continue paying for human experts.
2. Personalized legal intelligence: He says Hence Global uses AI to classify global news and connect it to individual lawyers' specialties and client portfolios, helping them notice otherwise-missed developments and contact clients proactively. He explicitly frames this as supporting, not replacing, lawyers' advice.
3. Analysis and marketing production: West says law firms already use the platform to draft client alerts, and that AI can generate branded newsletters reflecting a user's perspective. He identifies market-entry studies, travel-security briefings and scenario development as possible product directions rather than established capabilities.
4. Professional differentiation: As AI automates parts of legal work, West predicts an increasing need for lawyers to act as strategic advisors who understand political, legal and technological changes affecting clients.
5. Individual access to justice: West argues that AI-assisted demand letters and claim preparation can empower individuals dealing with institutions. He illustrates this with his own insurance dispute and describes courtroom legal robots in China that provide outcome estimates and enable claim filing.
6. Weaponized legal and regulatory processes: West predicts that near-costless lawsuit generation and filing could lead to millions of hostile lawsuits, including frivolous or fraudulent claims. He also argues that AI-generated regulatory comments can overwhelm administrative processes and delay rules.
7. Evidence and trust: West argues that widespread AI-generated falsehoods create a 'liar's dividend': people can dismiss authentic material as fake, undermining video evidence and, more broadly, trust and social relationships.
8. Political conditions and surveillance: West argues that AI's development and deployment are subject to political decisions that may accelerate, restrict or turn it into an instrument of geopolitical conflict. He also says AI makes it easier for governments holding large citizen datasets to conduct surveillance and classify people.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: West relies primarily on his advisory and product-building experience, reports about early adopters, personal anecdotes and examples discussed in his writing; he does not present systematic legal-AI performance or labor-market data.
pts.d:
1. Advice-market expansion rests on West's experience selling geopolitical advice and building Hence, together with his stated thesis that a very large market would pay a small amount for useful intelligence. No demand study or measured marginal-cost analysis is supplied.
2–3. Product claims are supported by his account of a handful of early-adopter law firms and their uses of Hence Global. For AI-generated publishing, he reports that an experimental Hence newsletter grew from zero to 1,000 followers in less than a week. These are founder-reported examples, not independent measurements of accuracy, time saved or client outcomes.
4. The strategic-advisor prediction is West's interpretation of legal automation; no staffing, hiring or revenue evidence is offered.
5. West reports that, after an insurer disputed his diagnosed concussion, he used a demand letter from Zaf Legal, which he describes as regulated in Utah. He says the insurer increased its initial offer tenfold within minutes. He also reports generating a possible complaint using a chatbot. This is a personal, pre-litigation anecdote, not evidence of a filed lawsuit or final settlement. His Chinese courtroom-robot example is a descriptive account without a named system, study or demonstrated accuracy rate; the 70% win estimate is illustrative.
6. For regulatory disruption, West recounts an example from his Harvard Business Review article: crypto-oriented lawyer activists released an AI comment-generation bot that produced over 100,000 comments on a Treasury proposal. He attributes delay of the rule to the resulting burden. The prediction of millions of hostile lawsuits is a projection, not an observed litigation count.
7. For evidentiary distrust, West recounts an episode involving video of Elon Musk and a defense that the recording could be a deepfake. He invokes the concept of the liar's dividend, attributed to unnamed lawyers, but gives no case citation, judicial finding or measured prevalence.
8. For surveillance, he points to China's social-credit system and says related developments are beginning in the United States, without presenting a detailed empirical study.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The interview mixes reported current uses in 2025 with undated future predictions. West conditions useful AI advice on current information, historical context and individual personalization, and conditions mass litigation abuse on extremely low filing costs.
pts.d:
1. Affordable automated geopolitical advice is presented as a current commercial opportunity, not a dated forecast of complete human-advisor replacement. West expressly preserves a premium market for human advice.
2–3. Hence Global is described as newly launched, with current emphasis on current-events intelligence, personal daily briefings, research and client communications. West says useful analysis requires understanding politics, business and the particular user's role and interests, supplemented by historical context. Market-entry studies, travel-security briefings and scenario generation remain prospective directions with no delivery dates.
4. Strategic differentiation is an ongoing-to-future prediction tied to other providers automating legal tasks; West gives no timetable, displacement percentage or claim that the whole lawyer role will disappear.
5. His demand-letter account concerns a past pre-litigation exchange. West characterizes it as involving no unauthorized practice of law; that is his qualification of the example, not a general legal conclusion about AI services. His positive access-to-justice assessment coexists with warnings about abuse, and he describes the Chinese systems as oriented toward encouraging settlement.
6. The hostile-lawsuit scenario is conditional on filing becoming effectively costless and has no specified date. The Treasury comment-generation example is described as occurring under the Biden administration and delaying a rule until the political environment changed.
7–8. Evidentiary distrust and surveillance are described as already emerging risks that may intensify. West says political processes can alter AI's trajectory, rather than treating technological progress as independent of governance.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups include law firms and individual practitioners, in-house lawyers and corporate buyers, individuals with unmet legal needs, litigation targets and regulators, and the wider public.
pts.d:
1. Businesses unable or unwilling to purchase expensive geopolitical advice gain a lower-cost route to intelligence. West particularly identifies sub-enterprise businesses, including those around $100 million or $1 billion in revenue, as exposed without sufficiently strategic internal legal resources. This is an enterprise-advice affordability claim, distinct from access to justice.
2–3. Law-firm lawyers can monitor multiple clients, identify relevant developments and initiate useful client contact; firms and solo practitioners can produce alerts and newsletters. In-house lawyers receive role-specific intelligence rather than a uniform corporate feed. Employment, intellectual-property and supplier-contract responsibilities are examples of different information needs.
4. Lawyers face increased pressure to distinguish their work from automated legal tasks through strategic advice. West sees an opportunity for general counsel and mid-career lawyers who develop geopolitical understanding, rather than specifying a numerical employment loss.
5. Individuals facing institutional resistance, exemplified by an insurance claimant, may gain practical negotiating and claim-preparation capacity without first retaining traditional litigation counsel.
6. People and organizations targeted by adversaries face potentially high-volume frivolous or fraudulent claims. Regulators face large AI-generated comment volumes that West says can impede rulemaking; activists acquire additional capacity to influence that process.
7. Lawyers relying on video evidence and participants in legal proceedings face authenticity disputes; the public faces wider erosion of trust in true information.
8. Citizens whose governments hold extensive personal data face AI-assisted surveillance and classification.
